claim: Rbfox1 is an RNA binding protein associated with intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism.
source: We found that upregulation of Rbfox1, an RNA binding protein associated with intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism, increases selectively hippocampal TrkB.T1 isoform expression.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to existing literature about Rbfox1's association with these conditions.

claim: Upregulation of Rbfox1 increases selectively hippocampal TrkB.T1 isoform expression.
source: We found that upregulation of Rbfox1, an RNA binding protein associated with intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism, increases selectively hippocampal TrkB.T1 isoform expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Increased Rbfox1 impairs BDNF-dependent LTP.
source: Physiologically, increased Rbfox1 impairs BDNF-dependent LTP which can be rescued by genetically restoring TrkB.T1 levels.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data presented in Figure 8.

claim: Impaired BDNF-dependent LTP caused by Rbfox1 upregulation can be rescued by genetically restoring TrkB.T1 levels.
source: Physiologically, increased Rbfox1 impairs BDNF-dependent LTP which can be rescued by genetically restoring TrkB.T1 levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Genes affected by Rbfox1 gain of function are different from those influenced by Rbfox1 deletion.
source: RNA-seq analysis of hippocampi with upregulation of Rbfox1 in conjunction with the specific increase of TrkB.T1 isoform expression also shows that the genes affected by Rbfox1 gain of function are surprisingly different from those influenced by Rbfox1 deletion.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis comparing gain and loss of function models shown in Figure 5.

claim: BDNF is secreted during Long Term Potentiation (LTP) induction.
source: BDNF is one of the most potent mediators of synaptic plasticity as it is secreted during Long Term Potentiation (LTP) induction and is functionally essential for acute signaling cascades leading to LTP [reviewed in Lu et al. (2013); Park and Poo (2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: BDNF is functionally essential for acute signaling cascades leading to LTP.
source: BDNF is one of the most potent mediators of synaptic plasticity as it is secreted during Long Term Potentiation (LTP) induction and is functionally essential for acute signaling cascades leading to LTP [reviewed in Lu et al. (2013); Park and Poo (2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: BDNF has a crucial role in cognitive functions.
source: As a consequence, BDNF has a crucial role in cognitive functions (Bambah-Mukku et al., 2014; Panja et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The Val66Met BDNF polymorphism impairs BDNF trafficking and synaptic localization.
source: This polymorphism impairs BDNF trafficking and synaptic localization, causes a reduction in activity-dependent BDNF secretion and is associated with alterations in brain structure and function leading to several neurological and psychiatric disorders (Greenberg et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Val66Met BDNF polymorphism causes a reduction in activity-dependent BDNF secretion.
source: This polymorphism impairs BDNF trafficking and synaptic localization, causes a reduction in activity-dependent BDNF secretion and is associated with alterations in brain structure and function leading to several neurological and psychiatric disorders (Greenberg et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Val66Met BDNF polymorphism is associated with alterations in brain structure and function leading to several neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: This polymorphism impairs BDNF trafficking and synaptic localization, causes a reduction in activity-dependent BDNF secretion and is associated with alterations in brain structure and function leading to several neurological and psychiatric disorders (Greenberg et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological manipulations of TrkB levels or activity result in impaired LTP.
source: Genetic or pharmacological manipulations of the levels or activity of the BDNF receptor Ntrk2 (TrkB) also result in impaired LTP and reduced synapse numbers causing deficits in the formation and consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memory (Minichiello, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological manipulations of TrkB levels or activity result in reduced synapse numbers.
source: Genetic or pharmacological manipulations of the levels or activity of the BDNF receptor Ntrk2 (TrkB) also result in impaired LTP and reduced synapse numbers causing deficits in the formation and consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memory (Minichiello, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological manipulations of TrkB levels or activity cause deficits in the formation and consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memory.
source: Genetic or pharmacological manipulations of the levels or activity of the BDNF receptor Ntrk2 (TrkB) also result in impaired LTP and reduced synapse numbers causing deficits in the formation and consolidation of hippocampus-dependent memory (Minichiello, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Hypomorphic expression of TrkB.FL causes hyperphagia-induced obesity due to reduced hypothalamic BDNF signaling.
source: Hypomorphic expression of the TrkB.FL causes hyperphagia-induced obesity due to reduced hypothalamic BDNF signaling, while genetic deletion of TrkB.T1 leads to increased anxiety related behavior associated with structural alterations in neurites of the amygdala (Carim-Todd et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Genetic deletion of TrkB.T1 leads to increased anxiety related behavior associated with structural alterations in neurites of the amygdala.
source: Hypomorphic expression of the TrkB.FL causes hyperphagia-induced obesity due to reduced hypothalamic BDNF signaling, while genetic deletion of TrkB.T1 leads to increased anxiety related behavior associated with structural alterations in neurites of the amygdala (Carim-Todd et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Up-regulation of TrkB.T1 levels in brains of a Ts16 mouse model leads to increased sensitivity of hippocampal neurons to BDNF deprivation.
source: Moreover, up-regulation of TrkB.T1 levels in brains of a mouse model with a Chromosome 16 trisomia (Ts16) leads to an increased sensitivity of hippocampal neurons to BDNF deprivation due to a block in TrkB.FL functions (Dorsey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Alterations in NTRK2 isoforms receptor levels have been associated with neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Importantly, alterations in NTRK2 isoforms receptor levels have also been associated with neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders (Dwivedi et al., 2003; Ernst et al., 2009a; Ferrer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The Ts16 mouse model has a TrkB.T1 upregulation despite having an intact Ntrk2 locus on Chromosome 13.
source: We took advantage of the observation that the Ts16 mouse model has a TrkB.T1 upregulation, despite having an intact Ntrk2 locus on Chromosome 13, to identify genes on Chromosome 16 responsible for the dysregulation of TrkB isoforms expression (Dorsey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Rbfox1 is expressed only in neurons, heart and skeletal muscle.
source: Rbfox1 is expressed only in neurons, heart and skeletal muscle, sites with notable TrkB expression.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Rbfox1 expression patterns.

claim: RBFOX1 dysregulation has been associated with intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy and Parkinson disease.
source: Moreover, RBFOX1 dysregulation has been associated with intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy and Parkinson disease, pathologies that have been associated with alterations in BDNF signaling as well (Chao et al., 2006; Conboy, 2017; Lu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Rbfox1 upregulation impairs hippocampal BDNF-dependent LTP by specifically increasing TrkB.T1 receptor levels.
source: We found that Rbfox1 upregulation impairs hippocampal BDNF-dependent LTP by specifically increasing TrkB.T1 receptor levels.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Rbfox1 can regulate the splicing and abundance of many gene isoforms in the nervous system.
source: Although Rbfox1 can regulate the splicing and abundance of many gene isoforms in the nervous system, we show that genetic reduction of the TrkB.T1 isoform in animals with up-regulated Rbfox1 is sufficient to restore hippocampal BDNF-dependent LTP, suggesting that Ntrk2 is a major target of Rbfox1 pathological dysregulation (Fogel et al., 2012; Gehman et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Li et al., 2007; Underwood et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Genetic reduction of TrkB.T1 isoform in animals with up-regulated Rbfox1 is sufficient to restore hippocampal BDNF-dependent LTP.
source: Although Rbfox1 can regulate the splicing and abundance of many gene isoforms in the nervous system, we show that genetic reduction of the TrkB.T1 isoform in animals with up-regulated Rbfox1 is sufficient to restore hippocampal BDNF-dependent LTP, suggesting that Ntrk2 is a major target of Rbfox1 pathological dysregulation (Fogel et al., 2012; Gehman et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Li et al., 2007; Underwood et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Ntrk2 is a major target of Rbfox1 pathological dysregulation.
source: Although Rbfox1 can regulate the splicing and abundance of many gene isoforms in the nervous system, we show that genetic reduction of the TrkB.T1 isoform in animals with up-regulated Rbfox1 is sufficient to restore hippocampal BDNF-dependent LTP, suggesting that Ntrk2 is a major target of Rbfox1 pathological dysregulation (Fogel et al., 2012; Gehman et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2016; Li et al., 2007; Underwood et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments and supported by the data.

claim: Overexpression of Tra2b in primary hippocampal neurons did not cause any change in TrkB isoforms expression.
source: However, infection of primary hippocampal neurons with a Tra2b-expressing lentivirus did not cause any change in TrkB isoforms expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Western blot analysis of primary hippocampal neurons transfected with a lentiviral vector expressing Rbfox1 showed increased truncated TrkB receptor levels.
source: Western blot analysis of primary hippocampal neurons transfected with a lentiviral vector expressing Rbfox1 showed increased truncated TrkB receptor levels associated with Rbfox1 overexpression while the TrkB.FL isoform was unaffected (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Rbfox1 overexpression in primary hippocampal neurons does not affect TrkB.FL isoform levels.
source: Western blot analysis of primary hippocampal neurons transfected with a lentiviral vector expressing Rbfox1 showed increased truncated TrkB receptor levels associated with Rbfox1 overexpression while the TrkB.FL isoform was unaffected (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: TrkB.T1 is the isoform upregulated by Rbfox1.
source: As shown in Figure 1A (right panel) western blot analysis with an antibody recognizing the specific 11 amino acid intracellular domain of TrkB.T1 confirmed that TrkB.T1 is the isoform upregulated by Rbfox1.
evidence: This is confirmed by western blot analysis using a TrkB.T1-specific antibody shown in Figure 1A.

claim: QPCR analysis revealed an increased level of TrkB.T1-specific mRNA while TrkB.FL was unchanged upon Rbfox1 overexpression.
source: Moreover, QPCR analysis also revealed an increased level of TrkB.T1-specific mRNA while TrkB.FL was unchanged, paralleling the results from the western analysis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: N-cre;Fox1 animals showed a modest 25% increase of Rbfox1 mRNA level in the hippocampus.
source: N-cre;Fox1 animals showed a modest 25% increase of Rbfox1 mRNA level in the hippocampus (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from mRNA analysis.

claim: N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi had a significant 35% increase in TrkB.T1 protein levels.
source: At the protein level, similar to what observed in vitro, N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi had a significant 35% increase in TrkB.T1 associated with about 33% Rbfox1 protein upregulation, while TrkB.FL level was unaffected (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi had about 33% Rbfox1 protein upregulation.
source: At the protein level, similar to what observed in vitro, N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi had a significant 35% increase in TrkB.T1 associated with about 33% Rbfox1 protein upregulation, while TrkB.FL level was unaffected (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: TrkB.FL level was unaffected in N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi.
source: At the protein level, similar to what observed in vitro, N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi had a significant 35% increase in TrkB.T1 associated with about 33% Rbfox1 protein upregulation, while TrkB.FL level was unaffected (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot quantification shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The levels of TrkC isoform receptors were unaffected by in vivo Rbfox1 upregulation.
source: To further test the specificity of this phenotype, we also investigated the protein levels of Ntrk3 (TrkC), another Ntrk family member also expressed in hippocampal neurons (Tessarollo et al., 1993), in the same N-cre;Fox1 hippocampi and found that the levels of TrkC isoform receptors were unaffected by in vivo Rbfox1 upregulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hippocampi from Rbfox1 heterozygous animals showed a significant 50% reduction in Rbfox1 protein levels.
source: Western blot analysis of hippocampi dissected from Rbfox1 heterozygous (Gehman et al., 2011) animals showed a significant 50% reduction in Rbfox1 protein levels.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis data.

claim: There was no change in TrkB.T1 or TrkB.FL receptor isoforms expression in Rbfox1 heterozygous animals.
source: However, there was no change in TrkB.T1 or TrkB.FL receptor isoforms expression (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Hippocampal lysates from Rbfox1 heterozygous animals showed a significant 35% upregulation of Rbfox2.
source: Hippocampal lysates from Rbfox1 heterozygous animals showed a significant 35% upregulation of Rbfox2 whereas Rbfox3 expression was unchanged [Figure 2A,B; (Vuong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Rbfox3 expression was unchanged in hippocampal lysates from Rbfox1 heterozygous animals.
source: Hippocampal lysates from Rbfox1 heterozygous animals showed a significant 35% upregulation of Rbfox2 whereas Rbfox3 expression was unchanged [Figure 2A,B; (Vuong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Rbfox1 is haploinsufficient.
source: This result strongly suggests that Rbfox1 is haploinsufficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Rbfox2 is upregulated in Rbfox1 heterozygous animals.

claim: Overexpression of Rbfox2 caused TrkB.T1 upregulation.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of Rbfox2 but not Rbfox3 caused TrkB.T1 upregulation as observed in N-cre-Rbfox1 transgenic mice (Figure 2C,D) suggesting functional redundancy at least in the context of TrkB.T1 receptor regulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Overexpression of Rbfox3 did not cause TrkB.T1 upregulation.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of Rbfox2 but not Rbfox3 caused TrkB.T1 upregulation as observed in N-cre-Rbfox1 transgenic mice (Figure 2C,D) suggesting functional redundancy at least in the context of TrkB.T1 receptor regulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Rbfox2 expression was not downregulated in response to increased Rbfox1 expression.
source: However, contrary to the upregulation of Rbfox2 caused by loss of one Rbfox1 allele, Rbfox2 expression was not downregulated in response to increased Rbfox1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Rbfox1 iCLIP experiments showed several iCLIP-hits along the Ntrk2 sequence covering both intronic as well as 3'-UTR regions of the gene.
source: Analysis of both HMW and soluble nuclear fractions showed several iCLIP-hits along the Ntrk2 sequence covering both intronic as well as 3'-UTR regions of the gene, suggesting direct binding of Rbfox1 to Ntrk2 transcripts (TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by iCLIP data analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Rbfox1 directly binds to Ntrk2 transcripts (TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1).
source: Analysis of both HMW and soluble nuclear fractions showed several iCLIP-hits along the Ntrk2 sequence covering both intronic as well as 3'-UTR regions of the gene, suggesting direct binding of Rbfox1 to Ntrk2 transcripts (TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from iCLIP data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RNA immunoprecipitation with anti-Rbfox1 antibody pulled down both TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1 mRNA.
source: While immunoprecipitation with control IgG failed to pull down any of the tested mRNA, IP with the anti-Rbfox1 antibody pulled down both the TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1 mRNA as well as a proximal intronic region upstream of the specific TrkB.T1 exon (Figure 3C), confirming the association found in the iCLIP experiments.
evidence: This is supported by RIP experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of Rbfox1 caused no change in the level of expression of TrkB.T1 containing the 3'UTR in HEK293 cells.
source: Surprisingly, despite the presence in the 3'UTR of six 'GCATG' Rbfox1 binding sites, expression of Rbfox1 caused no change in the level of expression of TrkB.T1 suggesting that the TrkB.T1 mRNA isoform is regulated by Rbfox1 through a different mechanism not involving the 3'UTR region.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TrkB.T1 mRNA, but not TrkB.FL mRNA, was significantly stabilized in primary hippocampal neurons by increased levels of Rbfox1.
source: Measurements of newly synthesized Ntrk2 mRNAs levels with basal or up-regulated expression of Rbfox1 showed that TrkB.T1, but not TrkB.FL mRNA was significantly stabilized (p = 0.03) in primary hippocampal neurons by the increased levels of Rbfox1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by pulse-chase mRNA stability assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Neither TrkC.FL nor TrkC.T1 mRNA stability was affected by Rbfox1 upregulation.
source: Testing of the same samples for Ntrk3 (TrkC) mRNA transcripts, showed that neither TrkC.FL nor the truncated TrkC.T1 mRNA stability was affected by Rbfox1 upregulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by QPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of Rbfox1-mutant lacking RNA binding capability failed to increase TrkB.T1 levels.
source: As shown in Figure 3E–F, overexpression of Rbfox1-mutant failed to increase TrkB.T1 levels suggesting that Rbfox1 RNA binding activity is essential for this function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Rbfox1 RNA binding activity is essential for increasing TrkB.T1 levels.
source: As shown in Figure 3E–F, overexpression of Rbfox1-mutant failed to increase TrkB.T1 levels suggesting that Rbfox1 RNA binding activity is essential for this function.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant experiment shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: RNA-seq analysis confirmed that TrkB.T1 mRNA was the only upregulated Ntrk2 isoform in N-cre;Fox1 transgenic animals.
source: More importantly, the RNA-seq analysis confirmed that TrkB.T1 mRNA was the only upregulated Ntrk2 isoform (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: TrkB.T1 (Ntrk2-202) and TrkB.FL (Ntrk2-201) isoforms are by far the most highly expressed in the hippocampus.
source: It also showed that among all the Ntrk2 isoforms annotated in the Ensembl database the TrkB.T1 (Ntrk2-202) and TrkB.FL (Ntrk2-201) isoforms are by far the most highly expressed in the hippocampus with approximately 15,000 and 12,000 reads respectively, whereas the other isoforms combined represent only about 5% of the total TrkB transcripts (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TrkB.T1 is the main truncated isoform expressed in the hippocampus.
source: In western blot analysis, an almost complete lack of signal at the level of the truncated isoform in the hippocampus of TrkB.T1 knockout mice also confirmed that TrkB.T1 is the main truncated isoform expressed in this region and no other truncated isoforms are present (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from TrkB.T1 knockout mice shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The major biological processes affected in the N-cre;Fox1 hippocampus are involved in important neuronal functions comprising synapse organization, neurotransmitter secretion, axonal development.
source: Gene ontology (GO) term analysis of the RNA-seq data revealed that the major biological processes affected in the N-cre;Fox1 hippocampus are involved in important neuronal functions comprising synapse organization, neurotransmitter secretion, axonal development and many others (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Bdnf is upregulated in the N-cre;Fox1 mouse.
source: Interestingly, we found that the TrkB-receptor ligand Bdnf is upregulated in the N-cre;Fox1 mouse although it is not clear whether this is the result of a compensatory mechanism in response to the upregulation of TrkB.T1 or whether Bdnf is a direct target of Rbfox1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The gene-isoforms that are differentially expressed in the hippocampus of N-cre;Fox1 mice are mostly different from the gene-isoforms affected by Rbfox1 deletion.
source: In fact, we found that the gene-isoforms that are differentially expressed in the hippocampus of N-cre;Fox1 mice are mostly different from the gene-isoforms affected by Rbfox1 deletion [Figure 5B; Supplementary file 1 and 2; (Vuong et al., 2018) (Gehman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Stimulation with BDNF showed an inverse correlation between TrkB.T1 expression levels and TrkB.FL (p-TrkB.FL) and ERK (p-ERK) phosphorylation.
source: Stimulation with BDNF showed an inverse correlation between TrkB.T1 expression levels and TrkB.FL (p-TrkB.FL) and ERK (p-ERK) phosphorylation suggesting an impairment in TrkB.FL signaling when TrkB.T1 is upregulated (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of TrkB.T1 in primary hippocampal neurons increased both basal as well as BDNF-stimulated p-TrkB.FL and p-ERK compared to control neurons.
source: Importantly, deletion of TrkB.T1 in primary hippocampal neurons increased both basal as well as BDNF-stimulated p-TrkB.FL and p-ERK compared to control neurons suggesting that TrkB.T1 expression levels are potent regulators of TrkB.FL signaling (Figure 6B,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C,D.

claim: TrkB.T1 expression levels are potent regulators of TrkB.FL signaling.
source: Importantly, deletion of TrkB.T1 in primary hippocampal neurons increased both basal as well as BDNF-stimulated p-TrkB.FL and p-ERK compared to control neurons suggesting that TrkB.T1 expression levels are potent regulators of TrkB.FL signaling (Figure 6B,C,D).
evidence: This is inferred from the TrkB.T1 deletion experiments shown in Figure 6B,C,D.

claim: Rbfox1 leads to a significant ~20% upregulation in TrkB.T1 but not TrkB.FL protein levels at the synaptic terminals.
source: Immunoblot analysis of hippocampal synaptosomal fractions from controls and N-cre;Fox1 mice showed that Rbfox1 leads to a significant ~20% upregulation in TrkB.T1 but not TrkB.FL protein levels at the synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is supported by synaptosome analysis data shown in Figure 7.

claim: N-cre;Fox1 animals had a blunted induction of LTP in response to BDNF.
source: Surprisingly, N-cre;Fox1 animals had a blunted induction of LTP in response to BDNF (Figure 8) and at 50 min this response was only about 30% of Ctrl (Ctrl 218.14 ± 22.42% vs. N-cre;Fox1 72.95 ± 12.82%) (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Introducing a TrkB.T1 KO allele in N-cre;Fox1 mouse model led to a significant, although partial rescue of the BDNF-induced LTP deficit.
source: As shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, this strategy led to a significant, although partial rescue of the BDNF-induced LTP deficit caused by Rbfox1 upregulation.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of BDNF-induced LTP in TrkB.T1 heterozygous animals (T1+/-) was similar to that of controls.
source: Interestingly, analysis of BDNF-induced LTP in TrkB.T1 heterozygous animals (T1+/-) was similar to that of controls, suggesting that TrkB.T1 is not haploinsufficient and its levels influence BDNF-induced LTP only in the situation of upregulation (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: TrkB.T1 is not haploinsufficient.
source: Interestingly, analysis of BDNF-induced LTP in TrkB.T1 heterozygous animals (T1+/-) was similar to that of controls, suggesting that TrkB.T1 is not haploinsufficient and its levels influence BDNF-induced LTP only in the situation of upregulation (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the heterozygous animal data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introducing a conditional TrkB.T1-loxP allele into the N-cre;Fox1 model led to a partial rescue of BDNF-induced LTP over time.
source: Importantly, this strategy also led to a partial rescue of BDNF-induced LTP over time, which became significant at 50 min (187.97 ± 49.26%) strongly suggesting that the TrkB.T1 up-regulation in neurons caused by Rbfox1 is causing the impairment in BDNF-induced LTP (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: The TrkB.T1 up-regulation in neurons caused by Rbfox1 is causing the impairment in BDNF-induced LTP.
source: Importantly, this strategy also led to a partial rescue of BDNF-induced LTP over time, which became significant at 50 min (187.97 ± 49.26%) strongly suggesting that the TrkB.T1 up-regulation in neurons caused by Rbfox1 is causing the impairment in BDNF-induced LTP (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is strongly suggested by the rescue experiments shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Analysis of the Shaffer collateral-CA1 excitability and presynaptic function showed no differences between the controls and mutant animals.
source: Analysis of the Shaffer collateral-CA1 excitability (Input/Output relationship Figure 8E) and presynaptic function with paired pulse stimulation (Figure 8F) showed no differences between the controls and mutant animals suggesting that hippocampal circuitries overall are not affected by the genetic manipulations.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: Hippocampal circuitries overall are not affected by the genetic manipulations.
source: Analysis of the Shaffer collateral-CA1 excitability (Input/Output relationship Figure 8E) and presynaptic function with paired pulse stimulation (Figure 8F) showed no differences between the controls and mutant animals suggesting that hippocampal circuitries overall are not affected by the genetic manipulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8E,F.

claim: Rbfox1 upregulation leads to a deficit in the BDNF-induced LTP caused, at least in part, by an increase in TrkB.T1 receptor expression.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that Rbfox1 upregulation leads to a deficit in the BDNF-induced LTP caused, at least in part, by an increase in TrkB.T1 receptor expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results.

claim: Upregulation or downregulation of a specific RBP can have different genetic outcomes.
source: These results suggest that upregulation or downregulation of a specific RBP can have different genetic outcomes and may be relevant to understanding how to approach pathologies caused by RBP dysregulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq comparison between gain and loss of function.

claim: Tra2b overexpression in transfected cells appears to increase splicing of SMN2 exon seven promoting the production of a full-length SMN2.
source: Tra2b overexpression in transfected cells appears to increase splicing of SMN2 exon seven promoting the production of a full-length SMN2, thus suggesting that this strategy could ameliorate SMA disease (Hofmann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Tra2b deletion in mice (Sfrs10−/−) does not influence splicing of SMN2 exon 7.
source: However, Tra2b deletion in mice (Sfrs10−/−) does not influence splicing of SMN2 exon 7 (Mende et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Decreasing only TrkB.T1 levels in the same cells where Rbfox1 is up-regulated is sufficient to restore BDNF-induced LTP.
source: However, decreasing only TrkB.T1 levels in the same cells where Rbfox1 is up-regulated, is sufficient to restore BDNF-induced LTP (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Bdnf expression is regulated at the transcription level by epigenetic factors and via the use of multiple promoters.
source: For example, it has been shown that at the transcription level Bdnf expression is regulated by epigenetic factors and via the use of multiple promoters.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about BDNF regulation.

claim: The neuronal spatially and temporally regulated processing of the pro-BDNF peptide provides another level at which BDNF function can be modulated.
source: In addition, the neuronal spatially and temporally regulated processing of the pro-BDNF peptide provides another level at which BDNF function can be modulated (Reviewed in Hing et al. (2018)).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The Val66Met BDNF polymorphism affects the processing and trafficking of BDNF and causes phenotypes including profound impairments in synaptic and cognitive functions.
source: The significance of this second regulatory mechanism has been validated by the Val66Met BDNF polymorphism in humans which affects the processing and trafficking of BDNF and causes phenotypes including profound impairments in synaptic and cognitive functions (Chen et al., 2005; Egan et al., 2003; Soliman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Almost nothing is known about the mechanisms regulating Ntrk2 expression or the mechanisms leading to its pathological dysregulation.
source: However, almost nothing is known about the mechanisms regulating Ntrk2 expression or the mechanisms leading to its pathological dysregulation (Kemppainen et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The Ntrk2 locus has only one promoter.
source: Contrary to the Bdnf gene that has multiple promoters activated by different stimuli, the Ntrk2 locus has only one promoter.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the Ntrk2 gene structure.

claim: The NTRK2 gene spans over 350 Kb of DNA sequence and allows for the generation, by alternative splicing of at least 36 potential transcripts from 24 exons.
source: The NTRK2 gene spans over 350 Kb of DNA sequence and allows for the generation, by alternative splicing of at least 36 potential transcripts from 24 exons (Luberg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Gene targeting experiments have shown that TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1 are the most highly expressed and phenotypically important during development.
source: However, gene targeting experiments have shown that two isoforms, namely TrkB.FL and TrkB.T1, are the most highly expressed and phenotypically important during development [Figure 4; (Dorsey et al., 2006; Fulgenzi et al., 2015; Klein et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research and data in Figure 4.

claim: No RBPs have been shown to regulate Ntrk2 splicing or mRNA transcripts levels prior to this study.
source: To date, no RBPs have been shown to regulate Ntrk2 splicing or mRNA transcripts levels.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Rbfox1 is the first gene shown to regulate Ntrk2 expression at the mRNA level.
source: Thus, Rbfox1 is the first gene shown to regulate Ntrk2 expression at the mRNA level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Rbfox1 directly binds to Ntrk2 RNA.
source: Its direct binding to Ntrk2 RNA (Figure 3C) and its function in promoting TrkB.T1 RNA stability, rather than splicing (Figure 3D) are strongly supported by: 1) the in vivo and in vitro Rbfox1 overexpression leading to up-regulation of only TrkB.T1 and no changes in TrkB.FL; 2) the confirmation of the change in expression of only TrkB.T1 by the RNA-seq analysis in N-cre-Fox1 mouse hippocampus; 3) the analysis of new nascent RNA showing that TrkB.T1, but not TrkB.FL RNA is more stable upon Rbfox1 overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by RIP data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Rbfox1 functions in promoting TrkB.T1 RNA stability, rather than splicing.
source: Its direct binding to Ntrk2 RNA (Figure 3C) and its function in promoting TrkB.T1 RNA stability, rather than splicing (Figure 3D) are strongly supported by: 1) the in vivo and in vitro Rbfox1 overexpression leading to up-regulation of only TrkB.T1 and no changes in TrkB.FL; 2) the confirmation of the change in expression of only TrkB.T1 by the RNA-seq analysis in N-cre-Fox1 mouse hippocampus; 3) the analysis of new nascent RNA showing that TrkB.T1, but not TrkB.FL RNA is more stable upon Rbfox1 overexpression.
evidence: This is supported by RNA stability data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The mechanism by which RbFox1 expression influences TrkB.T1 mRNA levels appears to be independent of an action on the 3'UTR region.
source: Nevertheless, the details of this newly identified molecular mechanism by which RbFox1 expression influences TrkB.T1 mRNA levels needs to be further elucidated since it appears to be independent of an action on the 3'UTR region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the hippocampus of Rbfox1 knock-out mice some genes lacking iCLIP clusters or GCAUG binding elements in the 3'UTR region can still be differentially expressed.
source: Importantly, this mechanism does not appear to be limited to TrkB.T1 since it has also been reported that in the hippocampus of Rbfox1 knock-out mice some genes lacking iCLIP clusters or GCAUG binding elements in the 3'UTR region can still be differentially expressed (Vuong et al., 2018) and Rbfox1 can increase the mRNA concentration of genes that lack identified 3'UTR miRNA binding sites (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Rbfox1 can increase the mRNA concentration of genes that lack identified 3'UTR miRNA binding sites.
source: Importantly, this mechanism does not appear to be limited to TrkB.T1 since it has also been reported that in the hippocampus of Rbfox1 knock-out mice some genes lacking iCLIP clusters or GCAUG binding elements in the 3'UTR region can still be differentially expressed (Vuong et al., 2018) and Rbfox1 can increase the mRNA concentration of genes that lack identified 3'UTR miRNA binding sites (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Upregulation of Rbfox1 has an inhibitory function on BDNF-induced synaptic plasticity most likely by reducing the TrkB kinase signaling through an increase of TrkB.T1 expression.
source: Upregulation of Rbfox1 has an inhibitory function on BDNF-induced synaptic plasticity most likely by reducing the TrkB kinase signaling through an increase of TrkB.T1 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Nervous system–specific deletion of Rbfox1 results in heightened susceptibility to spontaneous and kainic acid–induced seizures.
source: This is in line with the observation that nervous system–specific deletion of Rbfox1 results in heightened susceptibility to spontaneous and kainic acid–induced seizures which suggest increased neuronal excitability (Gehman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: There is increased evidence supporting a key role for TrkB activation in epileptogenesis caused by status epilepticus.
source: The presence of such regulatory mechanisms on TrkB function is important considering the increased evidence supporting a key role for TrkB activation in epileptogenesis caused by status epilepticus (McNamara and Scharfman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Rbfox1 regulates the splicing of several synaptic function genes including ion channels, neurotransmitter receptors, structural proteins of the synapse and vesicle fusion proteins.
source: Thus, having TrkB activity under the control of Rbfox1, which also regulates the splicing of several synaptic function genes including ion channels, neurotransmitter receptors, structural proteins of the synapse and vesicle fusion proteins, suggests a unifying biological system to regulate neuronal function and excitation (Gehman et al., 2011; McNamara and Scharfman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Reduced RBFOX1 expression has been associated with autism, epilepsy and heart disease in humans.
source: In humans, reduced RBFOX1 expression has been associated with autism, epilepsy and heart disease although the mechanistic relationship between RBFOX1 downregulation and these disorders is still unknown (Bill et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Impaired BDNF signaling has been associated with autism, epilepsy and heart disease.
source: Impaired BDNF signaling has also been associated with these diseases raising the interesting possibility that RBFOX1 regulation of the expression of TrkB receptors might, at least in part, be part of the pathogenetic mechanism.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about BDNF signaling in disease.

claim: Increasing or decreasing TrkB.T1-receptor levels affects BDNF/TrkB signaling.
source: Increasing or decreasing TrkB.T1-receptor levels indeed affects BDNF/TrkB signaling (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Nedd4-2 heterozygous mice have minimal developmental abnormalities such as hyperactivity, increased basal synaptic transmission and enhanced sensitivity to inflammatory pain.
source: For example, Nedd4-2 heterozygous mice have minimal developmental abnormalities such as hyperactivity, increased basal synaptic transmission and enhanced sensitivity to inflammatory pain (Yanpallewar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Human heterozygous missense mutations in Nedd4-2 cause major malformations including periventricular nodular heterotopia leading to hypotonia, intellectual disability, seizures, syndactyly and cleft palate.
source: However, human heterozygous missense mutations cause major malformations including periventricular nodular heterotopia leading to hypotonia, intellectual disability, seizures, syndactyly and cleft palate (Broix et al., 2016; Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Ntrk2 heterozygous mice do not show major abnormalities.
source: In addition, Ntrk2 heterozygous mice do not show major abnormalities while loss of one NTRK2 (TrkB) allele in human leads to hyperphagic obesity and severe impairment in memory, learning and nociception (Klein et al., 1993; Yeo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Loss of one NTRK2 (TrkB) allele in human leads to hyperphagic obesity and severe impairment in memory, learning and nociception.
source: In addition, Ntrk2 heterozygous mice do not show major abnormalities while loss of one NTRK2 (TrkB) allele in human leads to hyperphagic obesity and severe impairment in memory, learning and nociception (Klein et al., 1993; Yeo et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Neurons derived from iPSCs of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients have elevated RBFOX1 levels.
source: For example, it has been reported that neurons derived from iPSCs of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients have elevated RBFOX1 levels (Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Ablation of the Bdnf gene impairs the survival and/or maturation of substantia nigra (SN) dopamine (DA) neurons during development.
source: For example, ablation of the Bdnf gene impairs the survival and/or maturation of substantia nigra (SN) dopamine (DA) neurons during development (Baquet et al., 2005);
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Loss of one copy of Ntrk2 leads to an age-dependent increase in the levels of α-synuclein in the SN.
source: loss of one copy of Ntrk2 leads to an age-dependent increase in the levels of α-synuclein in the SN (von Bohlen und Halbach et al., 2005),
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: In a mouse model with a chronic reduction in TrkB signaling (~30% of WT) there is an age-dependent and selective degeneration of SN DA neurons and increased vulnerability of these neurons to neurotoxins.
source: and in a mouse model with a chronic reduction in TrkB signaling (~30% of WT) there is an age-dependent and selective degeneration of SN DA neurons and increased vulnerability of these neurons to neurotoxins (Baydyuk and Xu, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Neurons of PD patients have an increase in TrkB.T1 expression.
source: Because it has also been reported that neurons of PD patients have an increase in TrkB.T1 expression (Fenner et al., 2014), it will be of interest to test whether sporadic PD patients have RBFOX1 upregulation and, if that is the case, an association with increased TrkB.T1 receptor levels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: There is an intronic SNP affecting an enhancer in the fourth intron of RBFOX1 that leads to a substantial increase in expression.
source: In another study, it has been reported that in the human population there is an intronic SNP affecting an enhancer in the fourth intron of RBFOX1 that leads to a substantial increase in expression (Carter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: TrkB.T1 upregulation has been reported in neurodegenerative disorders.
source: While this SNP has been identified in the context of a study evaluating how inherited polymorphisms carried in the germline affect the somatic evolution of a tumor, it will be important to study whether this SNP has other effects on cognitive brain functions and leads to an increase in the incidence of neurodegenerative disorders where TrkB.T1 upregulation has also been reported (Cai et al., 2006; Dwivedi et al., 2003; Ernst et al., 2009b; Karege et al., 2005a; Karege et al., 2005b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The change in TrkB.T1 level caused by Rbfox1 upregulation is occurring at the synaptic terminals.
source: Most importantly, the change in TrkB.T1 level caused by Rbfox1 upregulation is not dramatic, but it is occurring at the synaptic terminals (Figure 7) which in turn can compromise critical BDNF functions on synaptic plasticity (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by synaptosome data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Gain of function mutations that facilitate or enhance the activation of protein kinase Cγ (PKC) by only approximately 10% have been associated with Alzheimer's disease.
source: For instance, gain of function mutations that facilitate or enhance the activation of protein kinase Cγ (PKC) by only approximately 10% have been associated with Alzheimer's disease (Alfonso et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: PKC is required for the synaptic depression caused by amyloid-β (Aβ).
source: PKC is required for the synaptic depression caused by amyloid-β (Aβ) and it has been suggested that a lifetime of slightly enhanced signaling may sensitize individuals to the detrimental effects of Aβ leading to AD (Newton, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.
